(Sūrat al-Shu'arā' is Meccan except verses 197 and from 224 to the end of the sūrah, which are Medinan; its verses number 227.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾ — read with the alif emphasized (tafkhīm) or inclined (imālah), and with the nūn made clear (idhhār) or assimilated into the mīm (idghām). This is either recited in a sequence of enumeration (ta'dīd) in the manner of a challenge (taḥaddī), according to one of the two views mentioned at the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah, in which case it has no place in i'rāb (grammatical analysis, i'rāb); or it is the name of the sūrah, as the majority agree, in which case its place is in the nominative (raf'), being the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhūf). This is more evident than taking it as the nominative of a subject (mubtada'), the reasoning for which has already been explained at the beginning of Sūrat Yūnus, peace be upon him. Or it may be in the accusative (naṣb) by supposing a verb appropriate to the context, such as "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 2:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾, "these" (tilka) is a reference to the surah, whether "Ta-Sin-Mim" (ṭasm) is recited as a enumerated sequence of letters or is a name for the surah, as its verification has already passed there. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is for the purpose of alerting to the elevated rank of what is pointed to in its magnificence. Its position is in the nominative, as it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is what follows it. And on the assumption that "ṭasm" is the subject, then it is a second subject (mubtada' thani) or a substitute (badal) for the first. The intended meaning of "the Book" (al-kitab) is the Qur'an, and of "the Clear" (al-mubin) is: the one whose inimitability is manifest; or, taking abana in the sense of baana (to be manifest), it is the one that clarifies the legal rulings and what relates to them; or it is the one that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. The meaning is: these are particular verses from it, singled out and designated by an independent name. And the intended sense of explaining that they are a part of it is describing them with the noble attributes for which the whole is renowned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 3:

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (bakhi'un nafsaka)﴾ That is: killing (qatil). The root of bakh' (slaughter to the point of severing the nukhā') is to carry slaughtering to the nukhā', which is a vein running inside the spine, and that is the furthest limit of slaughtering. It is also read "bākhi'u nafsika" with the genitive construction (idafah). And la'alla (perhaps) here expresses concern (al-ishfāq), meaning: be concerned for yourself lest you destroy it out of grief over what you have missed of your people's embrace of Islam.

﴿Not that they will not be believers﴾ That is: because of their not believing in this Clear Book, or out of fear that they will not believe in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If We will﴾, etc., is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for what is understood from the speech of the prohibition against the aforementioned grief, by explaining that their faith is not among the things upon which the will of God, Exalted is He, has definitively been set; so there is no basis for hoping for it or being pained by its loss. The object of the will is omitted because it is implied by the conditional response, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We shall send down upon them from the heaven a sign﴾, meaning: one compelling them to faith and forcing them to it. The fronting of the two adverbial phrases (zarfayn) before the direct object is, as has been mentioned many times, for the sake of giving importance to what is fronted (al-ihtimam bil-muqaddam) and arousing anticipation for what is delayed (al-tashwiq ila al-mu'akhkhar).

﴿So their necks remain bowed before it﴾, meaning: submissive. The original form is: "fa-zallu laha khadi'in" (so they would remain bowed before it), and the word "a'naq" (necks) was inserted to add emphasis by specifying the locus of humility, while the predicate was left in its original state. It has also been said: when "a'naq" was described with attributes of rational beings, it was treated like them in the grammatical form as well, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾. It has also been said: by it is meant the leaders and the groups, from the expression "jaa'anaa 'unuqun min an-nas" (a 'unuq of people came to us), meaning a company of them. It is also read as "khadi'atan" (feminine). His saying, Exalted is He: "fa-zallat" is coordinated (atf) upon "nunazzilu" with respect to its grammatical position (mahall).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, newly revealed, but they turn away from it﴾ is an explanation of the severity of their obstinacy and their failure to desist from their disbelief and denial, despite the compelling sign already mentioned, which should have turned the Messenger of Allah ﷺ away from his eagerness for their faith and cut off his hope in them. The first "min" (from) is extra (mazīda), for emphasizing generality, and the second is for the beginning of the end (li-ibtidā' al-ghāyah), figuratively, related to "ya'tīhim" or to an omitted element which is an attribute of "dhikr" (reminder). Whatever it is, it indicates its (the Qur'an's) excellence and nobility and the heinousness of what they did to it. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" serves to intensify the heinousness of their conduct and magnify their crime, for turning away from what comes to them from His presence, exalted and majestic is He, in absolute terms, is abominable and ugly, and turning away from what comes to them by the requirement of His pure mercy, exalted is He, for their benefit, is even more heinous and ugly. That is: no admonition from the Qur'anic admonitions, or any portion sent down from the Qur'an, that reminds them in the most complete reminding and alerts them from heedlessness in the most complete alerting, comes to them, as if it were itself the reminder from Him, exalted is He, by the requirement of His vast mercy, renewing its sending down as wisdom and benefit require, except that they renew their turning away from it, by way of denial and mockery, and persistence in the disbelief and misguidance they were upon. The exception is a truncated (mufarragh) exception from the most general of states, its place being in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of "ya'tīhim," with or without the implicit "qad," according to the well-known difference of opinion. That is: no reminder comes to them in any state except in the state of their turning away from it.

**﴿So they have indeed denied﴾**: that is, they denied the Reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, accompanied by mockery of it. They did not content themselves with turning away from it. Instead, they called it at one time sorcery, at another time fables, and at another time poetry.

The particle **فَ** (fa') in His words **﴿So there will surely come to them﴾** indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. The particle **سَ** (sin) emphasizes and affirms the content of the sentence. That is, **"there will surely come to them without any failure at all."**

**﴿the news of what they used to mock﴾**: the wording departs from what the preceding mentions of turning away and denial would require. This indicates that both of these accompanied their mockery, as was alluded to in His words: **﴿And no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them but that they turn away from it﴾** and **﴿They have denied the truth when it came to them, so there will come to them the news of what they used to mock﴾**. Its "news" (anbaʾuhu) is what will befall them of punishments, both immediate and deferred. It is expressed in this way either because these are things the Noble Qur'an has already informed of, or because by witnessing them they will come to know the true state of the Qur'an, just as they come to know hidden matters through hearing reports. In this wording there is also a magnification of the matter, since the word nabaʾ (news) is not applied except to a weighty report having a great impact. That is: **"there will certainly come to them the realization of what they used to mock before, without having reflected on its circumstances and paid heed to it."**

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 7:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) is for reproachful denial (al-inkar al-tawbikhi), and the waw is for coordination (al-'atf) upon an implied clause required by the context. That is: "Let them do what they have done of turning away from the signs, denying them and mocking them, and have they not looked﴿ at the earth﴾, i.e., at its wonders, which restrain them from what they have done and call them to turn towards what they have turned away from and to believe in it."

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿How many noble pairs of every kind have We caused to grow therein﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the signs in the earth that restrain from disbelief and call to faith. "Kam" is an informative (khabariyya) particle, in the accusative governed by what follows it as its object, and combining it with "kull" serves to convey both comprehensiveness and abundance together. "Min kulli zawjin" means "of every sort" (tamyiz, specification). "Karim" of anything is its pleasing and praiseworthy one; that is, many of every pleasing sort, abundant in benefits, which We caused to grow therein. The specific mention of its growth, to the exclusion of other kinds, is because it alone indicates both power and blessing together. It is possible that what is meant is all kinds of plants, both beneficial and harmful, and the description of all of them as "noble" is to draw attention to the fact that He, exalted is He, caused nothing to grow except that there is a benefit in it, as His saying, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ (Q 2:29). For the wise one hardly does an act except that there is in it profound wisdom, even if the heedless are unaware of it and the reasoning ones have not attained knowledge of its true nature.

**﴿Indeed, in that﴾** is a reference either to the verbal noun of "We caused to grow" (anbatna), or to each one of those pairs. Whichever it is, the distance implied in it serves to indicate the great distance of its rank in excellence.

**﴿is surely a sign﴾**: that is, a great sign, indicating the perfection of the power of the One who caused it to grow, the extreme abundance of His knowledge and wisdom, and the utmost breadth of His mercy, a sign that necessitates faith and restrains from disbelief.

**﴿And most of them were not believers﴾**: that is, most of his people, ﷺ, were not believers. It has been said: that is, in the knowledge and decree of God Most High, since He knew from eternity that they would turn toward evil in the choice that the matter of obligation (taklif) continually revolves around, and would not reflect upon these mighty signs. Sibawayh said: "kana" is a connecting particle (sila), and the meaning is: "and most of them are not believers." This is the more fitting with the context of explaining their obstinacy and their excess in stubbornness and opposition, despite the convergence of the factors necessitating faith from His side, the Exalted. As for attributing their disbelief to His knowledge and decree, it may be mistakenly understood from it that they are excused in it outwardly, because what has been pointed to of the verification is something that has been hidden from the expert, proficient scholars. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, in that is a dazzling sign necessitating faith, and yet most of them are not believers, owing to the extreme of their persistence in disbelief and error and their immersion in deviation and ignorance." And the attribution of non-faith to most of them is because among them are those who will believe.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is truly the Almighty﴾, the Overpowering over everything He wills among the affairs, of which taking vengeance against these people is among the parts. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, the one who abounds in mercy; therefore He gives them respite and does not seize them suddenly for the monstrous deeds they have dared to commit, which call for various kinds of punishment. In the mention of the attribute of Lordship (rubūbiyya) together with its attachment to his pronoun ﷺ, there is an honouring of him (ﷺ), and a hidden promise of vengeance against the disbelievers, which is not obscure.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 10:

﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to affirm what precedes it of their turning away from every sign that comes to them from the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah) and their denial of them, following the explanation of their turning away from the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah) that they witness. And "idh" is in the accusative (mansub)

(p-236)

as an object (maf'ulan bihi) of an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. That is: Recount to those who turn away and deny the time when He, exalted is He, called out to him, upon him be prayer and peace, and remind them of what befell the people of Pharaoh because of their denial of him, as a deterrent for them from what they are upon of denial, and as a warning lest there befall them the like of what befell their likes, the denying wrongdoers, so that it becomes clear to you that they do not believe in the signs that come to them. However, this is not merely by analogy of the state of these with the state of those, but by witnessing their persistence in what they are upon after hearing the revelation that speaks of their story and their failure to take admonition from it, as is hinted at by the repetition of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾ after every story. As for directing the command of remembrance to the time, although the purpose is to remind of the events that occurred in it, its secret has been explained many times.

﴿That come to﴾ meaning: "Go to" (ay i'ti), on the basis that "an" is explanatory (mufassirah), or "bi-an i'ti" on the basis that it is verbal (masdariyyah) with the preposition removed from it.

﴿The people of wrongdoing﴾ meaning: by disbelief and sins, and enslaving the children of Israel and slaughtering their sons. This is not the opening of what came within the scope of the call; rather it is what is detailed in Surah Ta-Ha from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾. The presentation of what occurred in a single story of statements in various expressions and differing styles has already been verified at the beginning of (Surat al-A'raf) at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Give me respite﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 11:

﴿Qawma Fir'awn﴾ (the people of Pharaoh) is either a substitute (badal) for the previous phrase, or an explanatory appositive ('atf bayan) to it. It was brought in to announce that they are a byword (‘alam) for wrongdoing, as if the meaning of "the wrongdoing people" and its rendering were "the people of Pharaoh." The restriction to mentioning his people is to announce the well-known fact that he himself is the first to be included in the ruling.

﴿Ala yattaqun﴾ (Will they not be mindful of God?) is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), brought in after his (peace be upon him) being sent to them as a warner, expressing wonder at their extremity in wrongdoing and their excess in transgression. It was also read with the second-person ta' of address (taqbil), following the mode of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which indicates an increase of anger against them. As if mentioning their wrongdoing led to addressing them directly with this, even though they were at that time absent (ghuyyab), yet they were treated as those present in the speech of the one sent to them, in that he conveys it to them and makes them hear it at the outset of their hearing it. This also carries additional urging toward taqwa for whoever reflects and contemplates. It was also read with a kasra on the nun, dispensing with the ya' of the first person (the speaker's ya'), and it has been permitted that it means: "Ala ya nas ittaquni" (O people, fear Me), like "an la yasjudu" (that they should not prostrate).

"He said" is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narration of what preceded, as if it were said: "What did Musa, peace be upon him, say?" So it was said: he said, humbly entreating Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾ from the very outset.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 13:

﴿And my breast will be constricted, and my tongue will not be eloquent﴾, coordinated with "I fear" (akhafu).

﴿So send﴾, that is, Gabriel, peace be upon him, ﴿to Harun﴾, so that he may be with me and I may be strengthened by him in conveying the Message. He, peace be upon him, based his request for this on three matters: the fear of being denied, the constriction of the breast, and the increase of what he suffered from the impediment of the tongue, through the withdrawal of the spirit into the inner part of the heart when he is constricted, such that he cannot speak. For when these come together, there is a need for a helper who strengthens his heart and takes his place when his impediment overcomes him, so that his mission is not disrupted and his proof is not cut off. This is not from making excuses or hesitating in receiving the command in any way; rather, it is a request for what will help him to carry it out, and a laying of the groundwork for an excuse concerning it. "And my breast will be constricted" and "my tongue will not be eloquent" have also been read in the accusative, coordinated with "they deny," in which case they are among the things he fears.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 14:

﴿And they have a charge of a crime against me﴾. That is: the consequence (taba'a) of a crime, so the modifying noun (al-mudaf, "consequence") is elided and the modified noun (al-mudaf ilayhi, "crime") is put in its place; or it is named by its own name. What is meant by it is the killing of the Qibti (the Egyptian). Calling it "a crime" is according to their claim, as his saying "to them" indicates. This is an allusion to a story set out at length in more than one place.

﴿So I fear﴾, that is: if I come to them alone, ﴿that they will kill me﴾ in retaliation for it before I have delivered the message as it should be delivered. This is not also a pretext; rather, it is a seeking of protection against an expected calamity before it occurs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, go both of you with Our signs﴾ is a narration of His response, exalted is He, to the two requests: the repelling (al-daf') understood from the deterrence (al-radc) from fear, and the joining of his brother (Harun), understood from addressing the discourse to both of them by way of predominance (al-taghlib). For it is conjoined (ma'tuf) upon an implied element (mudmar) indicated by the deterrence, as if it were said: "Be deterred, O Musa, from what you suppose, and go, you and whomever you have asked to be your helper." In His saying: ﴿with Our signs﴾ there is an allusion (ramz) to the fact that they will repel what he fears.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We are with you, listening﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the deterrence from fear and a further consolation to them both, by guaranteeing complete protection and support, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾. Here the one promised was in the presence of Pharaoh, so the "being with" was considered here. It was said: they were treated as the plural (ajraya majra al-jama'ah), but what precedes and follows it, with the dual pronoun, rejects this, i.e., "hearing what passes between you both and between him, so that We will make you victorious over him." He, exalted is He, is depicted by the state of one possessing might who has attended a dispute of a people, listening to what passes among them, in order to support his allies and make them prevail over their enemies, as an exaggeration in the promise of assistance. Or the "listening" (al-istima'), which means attentiveness (al-isgha'), is used metaphorically for the hearing (al-sam') which is knowledge of letters and sounds, and it is a second predicate (khabar thani). Or it is a predicate by itself, and "with you" (ma'akum) is an adverbial phrase of incomplete sense (zarf laghw).

The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾, is for arranging what follows it upon what precedes it, namely the gracious promise (of help). This is not merely an emphasis on the command to go, because its meaning is arriving at the one being approached, not merely heading toward it, like "al-dhahab" (going).

As for the singular "rasul" (messenger), it is either in consideration of the mission of each of the two of them, or because their request is one and the same, or because it is a verbal noun (masdar) that has been used as a description.

"And "an" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending (irsal) understood from "messenger" (rasul) includes the meaning of saying (qawl). And the meaning of their sending is: releasing them and leaving them to themselves, so that they may go with the two of them to al-Sham (Greater Syria)."

Pharaoh said to Moses, peace be upon him, after the two had come to him and said to him what they had been commanded. It is narrated that the two of them went to the gate of Pharaoh, but they were not admitted for a year, until the gatekeeper said: "There is a man here who claims that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds." Pharaoh said: "Admit him, perhaps we will laugh." So the two of them conveyed the message to him. Moses, peace be upon him, was recognized (p-238), and Pharaoh said at that point: ﴿Did we not raise you among us﴾ in our care and in our dwellings, ﴿as a child﴾, meaning as an infant; he expressed it thus because of the recency of his birth.

﴿And you remained among us for some of your years﴾. It is said that he remained among them for thirty years, then he left for Madyan and stayed there ten years, then he returned to them calling them to God, Mighty and Majestic, for thirty years, then he remained after the drowning for fifty years. It is also said that he struck the Copt when he was twelve years old, and fled from them as a result of that. And God knows best.

﴿وَفَعَلْتَ فَعْلَتَكَ الَّتِي فَعَلْتَ﴾ means: the killing of the Copt. After enumerating to him His favour in raising him and bringing him to the stage of manhood, He rebuked him for what had happened at the hands of killing his baker (*khabbaz*), and He magnified that and made it appear monstrous. It is read "*fi'lataka*" with a kasra on the fa', because it was a kind of killing.

﴿وَأنْتَ مِنَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ means: you were ungrateful for My blessing, in that you deliberately set out to kill a man from My chosen ones. Or it means: you were then among those whom I now count as disbelievers. [It is said that] he, peace be upon him, was falsely accused, or that his situation was misunderstood, since he was living among them through *taqiyya* (precautionary dissimulation of one's faith). Otherwise, where is he, peace be upon him, from sharing their religion? Accordingly, the sentence is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) relating to one of the two tā's. It is also permissible that it be a newly issued judgment against him: that he was a disbeliever in His divinity, or one of those who disbelieve in their religion, since they had gods that they worshipped; or that he was one of the ungrateful for blessings, one accustomed to denying them. Whoever is accustomed to that would not find such a crime to be a novelty from him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 20:

﴿He said﴾, answering him, confirming him regarding the killing and denying what he attributed to him of disbelief: ﴿I did it then, while I was among the astray﴾. That is: among the ignorant (jahilin). It has also been read: "So (it was) not that I was among the disbelievers," as you claimed falsely; that is, among those who do the deeds of the ignorant and the foolish, or among those who erred, since he did not intend to kill him but wanted to discipline him, or among those who went astray from what the striking (al-wakz) leads to, or among the forgetful (al-nasin), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest one of them should err, and the other remind her﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 21:

﴿So I fled from you﴾ to my Lord ﴿when I feared you﴾ that you would inflict harm upon me and hold me accountable for what I do not deserve, by my being guilty of the punishment.

﴿Then my Lord granted me judgment﴾ i.e., wisdom, or prophethood ﴿and made me one of the messengers﴾ — he [the verse] refutes, and by that [i.e., by this] he did not reproach him, disparaging his prophethood.

Then he turned back to what Moses had cited against him, namely the blessing, and did not state outright its rejection, since it was a truth that did not undermine his claim. Rather, he drew attention to the fact that this (blessing) was in reality a calamity. So he said: ﴿And this is a blessing with which you remind me of favor, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ That is: this upbringing which you cite against me as a blessing is, apparently, a favor; but in reality it is your enslaving the Children of Israel and your intent against them by slaughtering their sons, for that was the cause of my coming into your presence and of my being raised in your household.

It has also been said that the phrase is preceded by a hidden interrogative hamza of denial, meaning: "Or is it a blessing with which you remind me, namely that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?"

The position (i'rab) of ﴿an 'abbadta﴾ (that you have enslaved) is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to "ni'mah" (blessing); or genitive, with the preposition (ba') elided, or accusative, with that preposition elided.

It has also been said that "tilka" (this) refers to a hideous, unspecified trait, and "an 'abbadta" (that you have enslaved) is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) for it. The meaning is: your enslaving the Children of Israel is a blessing with which you remind me.

The shift to singular address in ﴿tamunnuha﴾ (with which you remind me) and plural address in what precedes it is because the reminder of favor comes from him alone, whereas the fear and flight were from him and from his chiefs (mala').

(p-239) ﴿Pharaoh said﴾ when he heard from him, peace be upon him, that firm statement and saw his steadfastness in his command and that he was not affected by the threats and intimidation he had presented, he began to object to his claim, peace be upon him, and started by inquiring about the Sender. So he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ This is a quotation of what occurred in his words, peace be upon him. That is: "What is the Lord of the worlds whom you claim to be His messenger," denying that there could be a lord of the worlds other than himself, as is indicated by his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ and his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾, and as his threat, uttered at the completion of his replies, peace be upon him, makes clear.

Moses, peace be upon him, replied to him: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾. This specifies what he meant by "the worlds," and the detailing serves to increase verification and confirmation, and to close the door on the accursed one's deception and his casting of doubt by taking "the worlds" to mean only what lies under his kingdom.

﴿If you are people of certainty﴾. That is: if you are people of certainty, verifying things and knowing them, then you know this; or, if you are certain of anything at all, then this is more deserving of certainty, because its evidence is manifest and clear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 25:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Pharaoh, upon hearing his reply, peace be upon him, out of fear of its influence on the hearts of his people and their submission to him.

﴿To those around him﴾ from among the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They were five hundred, wearing bracelets (al-asawir), which were reserved for kings alone."

﴿Do you not listen?﴾ showing off to them that what they have heard of his reply, peace be upon him, despite it being something unworthy of being taken into account, is a matter truly deserving of wonder. It is as if he said: "Do you not hear what he says? So listen to it and marvel at it, since he claims the opposite of a established matter that admits no doubt, intending by it his own lordship."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 26:

﴿He said﴾ (upon him be peace), making explicit what was already implied in his two previous answers: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾, and as a demotion of him from the claim to lordship (rububiyya) down to the rank of being a created one (marbubiyya).

Pharaoh said: when Moses, peace be upon him, confronted him with what was mentioned, that angered him and he feared the influence of his people from him. So he showed them that what he (peace be upon him) said is of the kind that does not proceed from sensible people, in order to turn them away from accepting it. So he said, emphasizing his shameful statement with the two particles of emphasis: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, in order to confuse them by this and divert them from accepting the truth. He called him "messenger" by way of mockery, and he attributed him to their addressing him, out of haughtiness, lest he should be a messenger to himself.

**﴿Said﴾** — he, peace be upon him, said: **﴿Lord of the East and the West and what is between them﴾**. He said this, peace be upon him, to complete and explain his first answer (p-240).

It also serves as an alert to their ignorance and their failure to understand the meaning of his statement. For the demonstration of God's lordship over the heavens and the earth and what is between them, although it includes a demonstration of His lordship over the two horizons (the East and the West) and what is between them, nevertheless, since it contained no explicit statement that the movements of the heavens and what is in them, the changes of their conditions and configurations, and the earth's being at one time dark and at another time illuminated, are ascribed to God Most High, He guided them to a way of knowing His lordship over what was mentioned. For the mention of the East and the West indicates the rising and setting of the sun, which are dependent on the movements of the heavens and what is in them, arranged in a wondrous pattern, whereby these firm conditions are ordered. All of these are originated matters, in need of an originator who is Powerful, Knowing and Wise, unlike the essences of the heavens and the earth, which the ignorant among the deluded may imagine to be independent of the existent who disposes them, because of their continuance.

**﴿If you were to understand﴾** — i.e., if you understand anything at all, or if you are among the people of intellect, you would know that the matter is as he stated. In this there is an announcement of the extreme clarity of the matter, such that it is not confused for anyone who has intellect at all, and an intimation that they are far removed from the circle of reason, and that they are the ones characterized by what they accused him, peace be upon him, of, namely madness.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 26, verse 29:**

﴿He said﴾. When the accursed one (Pharaoh) heard from him, peace be upon him, those statements founded on profound wisdom, and saw his firm resolve and the strength of his determination to carry out his command, and that he was one who could not be matched in the arena of debate, he turned away from engaging in fair discourse and inclined to the side of injustice and oppression. So he said, displaying what he had been concealing during the question and answer: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.﴾ He (peace be upon him) was not satisfied with Pharaoh's abandoning his claim to be a messenger and his not confronting him, until Pharaoh demanded that he (peace be upon him) take him as a god, out of the extreme of his arrogance and excess in what he possessed of the claim to divinity. This clearly indicates that his (Pharaoh's) astonishment and his mocking of the first answer, and his attributing madness to him (peace be upon him) in the second answer, were due to his (peace be upon him) attributing lordship to someone other than him. As for what has been said, that his question was about the reality of the Sender, and that his astonishment at the answer was because it did not correspond to his question, since the answer mentioned the Sender's attributes, this is not supported by the noble arrangement of the verses, nor by Pharaoh's situation, nor by his statement.

The lam in ﴿al-masjunin﴾ (the imprisoned) is the lam of previous reference (al-'ahd), meaning: "I will surely make you one of those whose condition you have known in my prisons," for he used to throw them into a deep pit until they died. For this reason, he did not say "I will surely imprison you."

"He said: 'Even if I come to you with something clear?'" That is, "Would you do this to me even if I come to you with something clear", i.e., manifest in confirming the truth of my claim. By this he means the miracle (mu'jizah), for it combines a proof of the existence of the Creator and His wisdom with a proof of the truthfulness of the one through whose hand it appears. Expressing it as "something" (shay') is for magnifying its importance. They said: the waw in "awa-law ji'tuka" is for the circumstantial state (hal), and the interrogative hamza has entered upon it, meaning: "while coming to you with something clear." I have mentioned many times before that it is for conjunction ('atf), and that the word "law" is not for the negation of a thing in the past because of the negation of something else in it. Therefore no apodosis is considered for it that has been omitted, relying on what precedes it to indicate it, as an intentional consideration, except when intending to explain the i'rab according to the technical rules. Rather, it is for showing the realization of what the preceding speech conveys of the judgment, affirmative or negative, in every supposed state among the states accompanying it, in general terms, by placing it upon the most remote of them and the most contrary to it, so that by its affirmation or negation together with that state, its affirmation or negation together with all other states becomes evident by way of priority (awlawiyyah). For whatever is realized together with a strong contrary, it is even more fitting that it be realized together with other things. For this reason, none of the remaining states is mentioned with it, and it suffices to omit them by mentioning the conjunctive particle joining the clause to its counterpart, which comprises all the states differing from it when they are many, so that what has been mentioned of the realization of the judgment in all states becomes evident. For when you say: "So-and-so is generous; he gives even if he is poor," you intend to show that giving is realized from him in every one of his supposed states, so you attach the judgment to the most remote of them, so that by its realization together with it, its realization together with all other states that have no contrariness to the judgment becomes evident by way of priority, which justifies suffice in omitting the detailing of them with the conjunctive particle. It is as if you said: "So-and-so is generous; he gives if he is not poor, and even if he is poor," i.e., he gives in the state of being rich and in the state of being poor. So the state in reality is both conjoined clauses, not only the one mentioned, on the basis that the waw is for the circumstantial state. The placing of the coming with what has been mentioned, with the word "law" rather than "in" (an), is not to show its improbability in itself, but in relation to Pharaoh. The meaning is: "Would you do this to me while I have not come with something clear and while I have come with it?"

Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have come with something, then bring it, if you are among the truthful.﴾ That is: in what your speech indicates, namely that you will bring something manifest, clarifying the truth of your claim, or of your claim to prophethood. The apodosis (jawab al-shart, the answer of the conditional clause) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 32:

﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ That is: its being a serpent was evident, not that it was something resembling a serpent. The derivation of "serpent" (thu'ban) is from "I made the water gush forth" (tha'abtu al-ma'a fa-nth'aba), i.e., I caused it to burst forth (fajjartuhu fa-nfajara), and the explanation of the manner of the state has already been given in (Surat al-A'raf) and (Surat Ta-Ha).

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ from his collar, ﴿and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾. It is said: when Pharaoh saw the first sign and said, "Do you have another than it?", he brought out his hand, and [Pharaoh] said, "What is this?" Pharaoh said, "Your hand. What is in it?" Then [Moses] put it into his armpit and then drew it out, and it had a radiance that almost dazzles the eyes and fills the horizon.

﴿He said to the chiefs around him﴾, that is, those seated around him. It is an adverb of place (*ẓarf*) standing in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). ﴿Indeed, this is a sorcerer, knowing﴾, surpassing others in the art of magic.

He wants to drive you out, by force, from your land with his magic. So what do you advise?" The authority of the miracle dazzled him (*bahharahu*) and bewildered him (*hayyarahu*), until it brought him down from the summit of claiming divinity (*rububiyya*) to the lowest depth of submitting to his own servants, as he supposed, and obeying their command. It brought him to the station of conspiring with them and consulting them, after he had been independent in opinion and governance. It also showed his sense of fear that they would seize his kingdom. Attributing the driving out and the land to them is meant to turn them away from Moses, peace be upon him.

(p-242) ﴿They said: "Delay him and his brother."﴾ That is, postpone their matter. It was also said: "Detain them." ﴿And send heralds into the cities to gather [the sorcerers]﴾ That is, police (*shurat*) who would gather the sorcerers.
﴿They will bring you﴾, that is, the summoners, ﴿every skilled, knowing magician﴾, one who excels in the art of magic. It is also read: "every magician" (bi-kulli sahir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 38:

﴿So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day﴾ This is what Musa (peace be upon him) specified with his words: ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment, and let the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾.
﴿And it was said to the people: "Will you gather together?"﴾ It was said to them this, urging them to gather and hastening them to hurry to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 40:

﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians, if they are the victors.﴾ That is: we will follow them in their religion, if they are the victors, not Musa, peace be upon him. Their intention by this was not that they would literally follow their religion; rather, it was that they would not follow Musa, peace be upon him. But they framed their speech in the manner of a metaphor (kinayah), so as to urge them toward earnestness and seriousness in the contest.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 41:

﴿Then when the sorcerers came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will we indeed have a reward,"﴾ that is, a great reward, ﴿"if we are the victors?"﴾ — not Musa, peace be upon him.

ي﻿Here is the translation:

﴿He said: "Yes indeed"﴾ [that is, you will have that], ﴿and moreover you will be among those brought near﴾ [to me]. It was said: he told them, "You will be the first to enter upon me and the last to leave from me." It was also read "naʿim" with a kasra on the ʿayn, and both are dialectal forms of the same word.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 43:

﴿Musa said to them﴾, that is, after the sorcerers had said to him: ﴿Either you throw, or we will be the first to throw﴾.

﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾. He did not intend by it a command to practice sorcery or to deceive, but rather a permission to present what they were definitely going to do, as a means of reaching the manifestation of the truth and the nullification of falsehood.

﴿So they cast their ropes and their staves, and said﴾: that is, they said it at the time of casting, ﴿"By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors."﴾ They said this because of their excessive confidence in themselves and because they had brought the utmost that magic could possibly achieve.

(p-243) ﴿So Moses cast down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up﴾, i.e., it swallows up swiftly. It has also been read as "talqafu" (تَلْقَفُ) with one of the two tā' elided from "tatalaqqafu" (تَتَلَقَّفُ).

﴿what they fabricate﴾, i.e., what they turn about from its true aspect and form through their deception and falsification, so that they make their ropes and staffs appear to be snakes moving about. Or "ifkuhum" (إفْكُهم, "their fabrication") is used as a name for that which is fabricated, for emphasis.

Verse 46: ﴿Then the sorcerers were cast down, prostrating.﴾ That is: immediately after they witnessed that, without hesitation or wavering, unable to restrain themselves, as though someone had cast them down, because they knew that such a thing lies beyond the bounds of sorcery, and that it is a divine matter that had appeared at the hand of him, upon him be prayers and peace, as confirmation of his prophethood. And in this is a proof that the utmost aim to which the endeavors of sorcerers can reach is deception, fraud, and the imagining of something that has no reality.

The Qur'anic quotation: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds."﴾

Translation of the commentary:

"They said, 'We have believed in the Lord of the worlds'" is a badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, an appositive in which the second term includes the first in meaning but is not identical to it) of "those who were thrown down," or it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) with "qad" (indicating past completion) understood before it.

The phrase of His, exalted is He, ﴿Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ is an apposition (badal) to "Lord of the worlds," serving to clarify it and to ward off the suspicion that Pharaoh is meant, since his ignorant people used to call him by that title. It also indicates that what compelled them to believe in Him, exalted is He, was the overpowering miracle He wrought at the hands of the two of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 49:

﴿Pharaoh said﴾ i.e., Pharaoh said to the magicians: ﴿Have you believed in Him before I give you permission?﴾ i.e., without my giving you permission, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Were the sea to be ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾ — not that permission from him was possible or expected.

﴿Indeed, he is your chief, who taught you magic﴾ — so you colluded in what you did; or, he taught you one thing and not another, and therefore he overcame you. By this he intended to confuse his people, lest they believe that they had believed with insight and the manifestation of truth. It has been read: "A-amantum" with two hamzas.

﴿So you will soon know﴾ — i.e., the consequence of what you have done. His saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all﴾ is an explanation of what he threatened them with.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 26, verse 50:

﴿They said﴾, that is, the magicians: ﴿No harm﴾, meaning there is no injury to us in it.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾ are a reason (ta'lil) for the absence of harm; that is, there is no harm in that, rather for us in it there is great benefit, due to what we gain by being patient under it for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, of expiation of sins (takfir al-khataya) and great reward. Or: there is no harm upon us in what you threaten us with of killing, for we must return to our Lord by one of the causes of death and killing, the least of which is that and the most hopeful of which is that.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 51:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers﴾. That is: because we were ﴿the first of the believers﴾, that is, the first among those who followed Pharaoh, or the first among the people of the assembly (al-mashhad). This is a second justification (ta'lil) for the negation of harm (nafy al-dayr), meaning: there is no harm upon us in your killing (of us). "Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins because we are the first of the believers." It has been read as ﴿in kunna﴾ (if we were), as a conditional (al-shart), for the sake of humbling oneself (hadm al-nafs) and not being confident of the outcome (al-khatima); or in the manner of the speech of one who relies upon his own standing, like the words of a worker to an employer who delayed his wage: "If I have worked for you, then pay me my due."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 52:

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants."﴾ This was after Moses had remained among them for some years, calling them to the truth and showing them the signs, but they increased in nothing except obstinacy (ʿutuww) and stubbornness (ʿinad), as was detailed in (Surat al-A'raf) with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]...﴾ and the verses that follow. It is also read with a kasra on the nun and a waslah on the alif, from "sara" (to travel by night), and it is read: "Anis-ir" (ans sir), from al-sayr (travel).

﴿Indeed, you are being pursued﴾ is a justification for the command to travel by night, i.e., Pharaoh and his soldiers will follow you at dawn, so travel with those who are with you, so that they do not overtake you before you reach the sea, and so that they do not enter your entrances, whereupon I would close it over them and drown them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 53:

﴿Then Pharaoh sent﴾ when he was informed of their departure ﴿into the cities, gatherers﴾, gathering the troops so that they would follow them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 54:

﴿Indeed, these⁠﴾ means: the Children of Israel, ﴿are but a small band﴾ — he belittled them, though they were six hundred thousand and seventy thousand in comparison to his armies. It is related that he sent in pursuit of them one million and five hundred thousand angel-guarded troops (musawwar), with every (commander) having a thousand (men). Pharaoh went out with a great host, and his vanguard was seven hundred thousand men on horses, with a helmet (bayda) on his head. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Pharaoh went out with one million horses, apart from the mares.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 55:

﴿And indeed they are enraging us﴾ That is: doing that which enrages us.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 56:

﴿And indeed, we are all alert and cautious.﴾ He means: because of their small number, he does not care for them, nor does he expect their victory or their superiority. Rather, they do deeds that enrage us and constrict our chests, while we are a people whose custom is vigilance, caution, and the use of firmness in affairs. So when someone rebels against us, we hasten to extinguish the flame of his corruption. These are excuses he offered to the people of the cities, lest it be suspected of him that something would diminish his subjugation and authority.

It is also read: "ḥadhirūn" (ḥādhirūn with a dhāl-less ending), where the first (ḥādhirūna) indicates renewal (tajaddud), and the second (ḥadhirūn) indicates permanence (thabāt). It is said: al-ḥādhir means one who is equipped with weapons (al-mu'addī fi al-silāh). It is also read: "ḥādirūn" with an unpointed dāl (ḥ-d-r), meaning: strong and fierce (aqwiyā' wa-ashiddā'). It is said: fully armed with weapons (mudajjajūn fi al-silāh), having acquired that hardness in their bodies (qad kasabahum dhālika ḥidāratan fi ajsāmihim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verses 57–58:

﴿So We expelled them﴾ by creating in them the impetus (*da'iyah*) to leave for this reason, so We carried them over to them.

﴿from gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station﴾ all of that belonged to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verses 57–58:

﴿So We expelled them﴾ by creating in them the impetus (*da'iyah*) to leave for this reason, so We carried them over to them.

﴿from gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station﴾ all of that belonged to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 59:

(p-245) ﴿Thus⦆ is either a comparative verbal noun (masdar tashbihi) for "We expelled", meaning: "We expelled them with a similar wondrous expulsion", or it is a qualifier of "a noble station", meaning: "from a noble station that was such", or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning: "the matter is thus."

﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them⦆: that is, We made them possess it, in the manner of the transfer of a deceased person's property to his heir, as though they had owned it from the time its former owners went out from it, before they had taken possession of it and received it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 60:

﴿So they followed them﴾, i.e., they caught up with them. It is also read "fa-ittaba'uhum" (with a doubled ta', the verb being tab'a, "to follow", in the form ittaba'a).

﴿at sunrise﴾: entering the time of the sun's rising, i.e., its emergence (tulu').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 61:

﴿Then when the two hosts saw each other﴾ they drew so close that each of the two groups saw the other. It is also read: "تَراءَتِ الفِئَتانِ" (taraāti al-fi'atān, "the two companies saw each other," with the verb feminine to agree with the feminine plural noun al-fi'atān).

﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are overtaken."﴾ They used the nominal sentence reinforced with two particles of emphasis (inna and the lam of emphasis), to indicate the certainty of the overtaking and catching up, and that both were imminent. It is also read: "لَمُدَّرِكُونَ" (lamudarrikūn), with the dal doubled, from idrāk al-shay' (ادّراك الشيء), meaning: when a thing follows continuously until it is finished; that is, "indeed, we are being continuously destroyed at their hands" (lamutatābi'ūn fī al-halāk 'alā aydīhim).

"Qāla kallā" (﴿قالَ كَلا﴾): Said [Moses]: "Never!" Withdraw from that [thought], for they will not overtake you. "Inna maʿiya Rabbī" (﴿إنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي﴾): Indeed, my Lord is with me, with [His] help and guidance. "Sa-yahdīn" (﴿سَيَهْدِينِ﴾): He will surely guide me, absolutely, to the path of deliverance from them entirely.

It is narrated that Yusha' (Joshua), upon him be peace, said: "O Kalim Allah (Interlocutor of God), where are you commanded [to go]? For Pharaoh has overtaken us, and the sea is before us." He, upon him be peace, said: "Here." So Yusha' (upon him be peace) plunged into the water, and Musa (upon him be peace) struck the sea with his staff, and what happened, happened.

A believer from the family of Pharaoh was standing before Musa (peace be upon him), and he said: "Where have you been commanded to go? For this sea is before you, and the people of Pharaoh have overtaken you." Musa (peace be upon him) said: "I have been commanded to go by the sea, and perhaps I shall be shown what to do, so I shall act upon what I am commanded." This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff."﴾ — (the sea being) al-Qulzum, or the Nile. ﴿And it parted﴾ — the fa' (in fa-infalaqa) is fasihah (indicating an implied step), meaning: he struck it, and it parted, becoming twelve paths, according to the number of the tribes (asbat), with passages between them.

﴿And each part became﴾ — resulting from the splitting — ﴿like a mighty mountain﴾, like a lofty mountain, firm in its place. So they entered its ravines, each tribe into one of its ravines.

ترجمة:

﴿And We brought near﴾, that is: We drew close, ﴿there the others﴾, that is: Pharaoh and his people, until they entered in their wake into their own entryways.
And We delivered Moses and those with him, all of them, by preserving the sea in that state until they crossed over to the land.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 66:

(p-246) ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ by the closing of the sea over them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 67:**

﴿Indeed, in that﴾: that is, in all that has been detailed of what issued from Musa, upon him be peace, and what manifested at his hands of overwhelming miracles, and of what Pharaoh and his people did of words and deeds, and what was done to them of punishment and retribution. The sense of distance contained in the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) serves to magnify and horrify the matter indicated, just as the indefiniteness of "sign" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a sign﴾, means: what a sign it is, or: a great sign that cannot quite be described, one that obliges those who take heed to learn from it and to measure the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the affair of Musa (upon him be peace), and their own condition against the condition of those destroyed. It obliges them to refrain from engaging in the disbelief, sins, and opposition to the Messenger in which they were engaged, to believe in God, exalted is He, and to obey His Messenger, so that there does not befall them the like of what befell those. Or: in what has been detailed of the story, in respect of the Messenger's relating it upon him be blessings and peace exactly as it is, without having heard it from anyone, is a great sign indicating that this comes through true revelation, obliging belief in God alone and obedience to His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿Yet most of them were not﴾: that is, most of those who heard their story from him, upon him be blessings and peace, ﴿believers﴾, neither by measuring his affair against the affair of Musa, upon them both be peace, and their own condition against the condition of those deniers who were destroyed, nor by reflecting on his relating their story without having heard it from anyone, although each of the two routes is one that certainly leads to faith. The meaning of "most of them were not believers" is: how few of them were believers. This is on the basis that "kana" is redundant (za'ida), as is the view of Sibawayh, so that it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Most people will not believe, however eager you are﴾. This is a report from Him, exalted is He, of what would occur from the polytheists after they heard the verses clearly recounting the story, confirming what came earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Never does a fresh reminder come to them from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it﴾, and ﴿They have indeed denied...﴾ and so on. The choice of the nominal sentence serves to indicate their firm establishment in non-belief and their persistence in it. It is also permissible to take "kana" in the sense of "became" (sara), as was done in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he was among the disbelievers﴾. The meaning then is: most of them did not become believers, despite hearing the great sign that obliges it in the two ways mentioned. In that case the report is of their not becoming (believers) before the event occurred, to indicate the full realization and firm establishment of it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The command of God has come...﴾, the verse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 68:

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty﴾ (al-'Aziz), the One who prevails over everything He wills, among the matters of which is taking vengeance upon those who deny. ﴿The Merciful﴾ (al-Rahim), the one who is exceedingly merciful. For this reason He gives them respite and does not make their punishment, for not believing after witnessing this great sign by way of revelation, [immediate], despite their full deserving of it. This is what the eloquence of the noble composition requires, from the beginning of the noble surah to the end of the seven stories, and indeed to the end of the noble surah, as a clear implication beyond doubt. As for what has been said, that the pronoun in "aktharuhum" (most of them) refers to the people of Pharaoh's era from the Copts and others, and that the meaning is: "Most of the people of Egypt were not believers, since none of them believed except Asiya, Hizqil, and Maryam, daughter of Yamusha, who pointed to the coffin of Yusuf (peace be upon him). And the Children of Israel, after they were saved, asked for a cow to worship and took the calf, and said: 'We will not believe you until we see God openly'" — this is far from verification. How could it be otherwise, when the thrust of each of the stories in the noble surah, other than the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is merely to explain the condition of a specific group who defied the command of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers (peace and blessings be upon them), as is made clear by the introduction of the stories with their denial of the messengers after they had witnessed with their own eyes the great signs that obligate belief and restrain them from disbelief and disobedience, yet they persisted in what they were upon of denial. So God Most High punished them for that with worldly punishment and cut off their last trace entirely. How then is it possible that He would report about them that most of them did not believe, especially after reporting their destruction, and counting the believers among them at first and excluding them from it at last, while they did not share with them at all in any of the crimes reported of them, which obligates exalting the Revelation above the likes of this? So reflect.

﴿And recite to them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the implied verb that is understood as the operative element for "when he called out…" and so on. That is: and recite to the polytheists ﴿the account of Abraham﴾, i.e., his great and momentous story, as it was revealed to you, so that you may stand upon what was mentioned of their not believing in the signs that come to them by one of the two ways.

Here is the translation:

﴿Idh qala﴾ is in the accusative, either as an adverbial of time governed by "al-naba'" (the report), meaning: "recount to them the report at the time he said to his father and his people:" ﴿to his father and his people﴾; or as an object of "utlu" (recite), in which case it is a substitute (badal) for "naba'," meaning: "and recite to them at the time he said to them:" ﴿What do you worship?﴾ On this reading, what is recited is what he said to them at that time, when he (peace be upon him) asked them about it, so that on their answer he would build the point that what they worship has no claim whatsoever to worship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 71:

﴿They said: "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ They did not limit themselves to the adequate answer of simply saying "idols," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: "The surplus."﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: "What has your Lord sent down?" They said: "Goodness," and their like, but rather they expanded upon it by stating the verb and conjoining the continuance of their devotion to their idols, intending thereby to display what was in their wicked souls of delight and boastfulness in that. The meaning of al-zulul (ظلول, "remaining") is continuance (al-dawam). It was also said: they worshipped them by day and not by night. The complement of al-'ukuf (العكوف, "devotion") is the word "ʿalā" (على, "upon"), and the introduction of the lam (اللام, "for") serves to convey an additional meaning, as if they had said: "we remain for their sake, turned towards their worship, or circling around them." This too is part of their expansiveness (ītnāb).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 72:

﴿Said he﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) answering a question that arises from the detail of their answer. ﴿Do they hear you?﴾ That is: do they hear your supplication (du'a')? This is with an elision of the modifier (al-mudaf), or it means: do they hear you while you call upon them, as in your saying, "I heard Zayd say such and such," where the object is elided because of the indication of His Exalted saying: ﴿when you call﴾ upon it.

It has been recited as "Do they make you hear?" (hal yusmi'unakum) from the causative form (al-isma'), meaning: do they make you hear anything of things, or an answer to your supplication, and can they do that? The present-tense form with "when" (idh) is for the narration of a past state (hikayat al-hal al-madiyah) in order to bring its image to mind, as if it were said to them: recall the past circumstances in which you used to invoke them, and answer: did they hear, or did they ever hear?

"Or do they benefit you," by reason of your worshipping them? "Or do they harm you?" That is: they harm you by your abandoning their worship, since worship must have something (a purpose) to it, especially when it is carried out, as you have described, with such intensity, in the hope of bringing benefit or warding off harm.

They replied: "No, we found our fathers doing thus." They admitted that these idols were utterly incapable of what had been mentioned, of hearing, benefit and harm, and they were compelled to make plain that they had no support save imitation (taqlid): that is, "We did not know, nor did we see from them any of the matters mentioned; rather, we found our fathers doing thus," that is, worshipping as we worship, so we followed them.
﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping?"﴾ That is: Have you looked and thus seen, or have you reflected and thus known what you used to worship?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 76:

﴿You and your forefathers, the ancients﴾ [are the object of] true sight (ḥaqq al-ibṣār) or true knowledge (ḥaqq al-ʿilm).

His saying, ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾, explains the state of what they worship, after alerting them to their lack of knowledge of this. That is, know that they are enemies to their worshippers, who love them as the love of Allah, the Exalted, because they are harmed by them far more than a man is harmed by his enemy. Or it is because the one who incites them to worship these idols and compels them to it is Satan, who is the greatest enemy of humankind. However, he (peace be upon him) presented the matter as concerning himself, as an indirect allusion to them, since that is more effective in advice than explicit statement, and as an indication that it is advice which he began with himself, so that it would be more likely to be accepted. "ʿAduww" (enemy) and "ṣadīq" (friend) may be used for both the singular and the plural. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they are an enemy to you﴾, where it is treated like the verbal nouns (maṣādir) for the sake of balance, like al-qabūl (acceptance), al-walūʿ (eagerness), al-ḥanīn (yearning), and al-ṣahīl (neighing).

﴿Except the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but the Lord of the worlds is not like that. Rather, He is my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter, who never ceases to bestow His favours upon me with their benefits, as is indicated by what He, Exalted is He, has described Himself with of the rulings of guardianship. It was also said that it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), and this is the view of al-Zajjāj, on the basis that the pronoun refers to every deity worshipped, and some of their forefathers had worshipped Allah, Exalted is He.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 78:

And His saying, ﴿Who created me﴾, is an attributive description of "the Lord of the worlds," and He made it the subject (mubtada') with what follows it as the predicate (khabar). This is not befitting the eloquence (jizalah) of the revelation. Rather, He, exalted is He, described Him with that and with what He conjoined to it, although all of it falls under His lordship over the worlds, explicitly stating the blessings specific to him, peace be upon him, and detailing them, because they are more effective in requiring that worship be devoted exclusively to Him, exalted is He, and in restricting the seeking of refuge, for the attainment of religious and worldly benefits and the averting of immediate and deferred harms, to Him, exalted is He.

(p-249) ﴿So it is He who guides me﴾, meaning: He alone guides me to everything that concerns me and sets me right in matters of religion and worldly life, a guidance connected to the moment of creation and the breathing in of the spirit, renewed continuously, as indicated by the fa' (so) and the present-tense form. For He, exalted is He, guides everything He created to what it was created for, among the affairs of livelihood and the hereafter, a guidance progressing from the beginning of its existence to the end of its term, by which it is enabled to attract its benefits and ward off its harms, either by nature or by choice. Its beginning, with respect to the human being, is the guidance of the fetus to suck the blood of menstruation, and its end is the guidance to the path of Paradise and enjoyment of its everlasting bliss.

ۚ "And the One who feeds me and gives me drink" — this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the first attribute. The repetition of the relative pronoun (al-ladhi) in the three positions, along with the sufficiency of conjoining what occurs within the relative clause's scope of the six sentences upon the relative clause of the first relative pronoun, is to signal (li-l-idhan) that each one of those relative clauses is a sublime description of Him, exalted, independent in necessitating the ruling in reality, deserving that it apply to Him, exalted, on its own, and not be made to follow after others.

Note on the source: the passage's first phrase is quoted from Qur'an 26:79 as ﴿والَّذِي هو يُطْعِمُنِي ويَسْقِينِ﴾, rendered above as "And the One who feeds me and gives me drink."

Translation of the Arabic terms:
- ʿatf: conjunction (coordination) of a following word or clause onto a preceding one.
- al-ṣifa al-ūlā: the first attribute.
- al-mawṣūl: the relative pronoun.
- ṣila: the relative clause.
- iʾdhan: a signal or indication.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 80:

﴿And when I fall ill, it is He who cures me.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "who feeds me and gives me drink" (yuṭʿimunī wa-yasqīn), and the three were arranged together under one relative clause (silat al-ṣilah) for a single relative pronoun, because health and sickness are for the most part consequences of eating and drinking. The attribution of sickness to oneself and of healing to God, the Exalted, although both come from Him, Exalted is He, is in observance of good manners (ḥusn al-adab), as the Khidr, peace be upon him, said: ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ and said: ﴿So your Lord wished that they should reach their maturity﴾.

As for causing death, since it is among the greatest of His exclusive attributes, like giving life, both at the beginning and in return, and since all the affairs of the Hereafter, along with what follows them of resurrection, are attached to it, He strung both together in one thread in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who will cause me to die, then bring me to life﴾. This is so because death, being a means to attaining eternal life, is far from being something not natural to him, peace and blessings be upon him.

The phrase ﴿And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ is mentioned by him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), as a display of humility (*hadm*) toward himself and as instruction for the community, that they should avoid sins, be cautious, and seek forgiveness for what slips from them. It also serves to guard against whatever minor lapses (*saghair*) might occur from him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), and as a warning to his father and his people that they should reflect on their own affairs and realize that they are in a state of wretchedness beyond measure. For his state, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), even while he was in the utmost degree of obedience to God Most High and worship of Him, and was at that rank, then what do you think of the state of those who were immersed in disbelief and all kinds of sins and errors?

As for taking the sin to refer to his three statements, ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ and ﴿Rather, the largest of them did it﴾, and his saying to Sarah, "She is my sister," this is impossible, because these were allusive statements (*ma'arid*, indirect speech that is not literally false), not of the kind of sins that require seeking forgiveness. They issued from him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), after this dispute that took place between him and his people. As for the third, it is clear, since it occurred after his emigration, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), to (p-250) Syria. As for the first two, they occurred while the idols were being broken. And it is evident that the exchange of these statements among them was at the beginning of the matter. Hanging the forgiveness of the sin on the Day of Recompense, although forgiveness is granted in this world because its effect becomes manifest on that day, is also because that conveys a sense of awe for him and an indication that the requital will take place on that day if it is not forgiven.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 83:

﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom﴾ after he (peace be upon him) had mentioned to them the manifold kindnesses bestowed upon him by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the beginning of his creation until the day of his resurrection, which moved him to converse with Him, may He be exalted, and to supplicate Him, seeking to secure what he already has (al-'atid) and to attract what is yet more (al-mazid). And ḥukm (judgment/wisdom): the ḥikmah (wisdom), which is perfection in knowledge and action, such that by it one is able to take up the vicar-ship of the Truth (khilafat al-Haqq) and leadership over creation (riyasat al-Khalq).

﴿And join me with the righteous﴾: and grant me, from knowledge, deeds and dispositions, that which qualifies me to be ranked within the company of the perfected, those firmly established in righteousness, who are free from the major and minor sins. Or, gather me and them together in Paradise. And indeed Allah answered him when He said: ﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 84:

﴿And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ That is: a standing and good repute in this world, such that its trace remains until the Day of Religion (yawm al-din, the Day of Judgment). For this reason you do not see any nation among the nations except that it loves him and praises him. Or (it means) a truthful one from my offspring who will establish the foundation of my religion (usul dini) and call people to what I used to call them to of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), and he is the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham﴾.
"And make me" in the Hereafter "among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss." The sense of inheritance (al-wirathah) has already been explained in (Surat Maryam).

﴿And forgive my father﴾ by guiding him and granting him success in faith, as is hinted at by the reason given in His words: ﴿Indeed, he was among the astray﴾, meaning those who strayed from the path of truth. The full investigation of this matter has already been presented in the exegesis of Surat al-Tawbah and Surat Maryam, in a way that admits of nothing further.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 87:

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾ by reproaching me for what I neglected, or by diminishing my rank among the heirs (al-wurrath), or by punishing me while the outcome is hidden and punishment is rationally permissible; all of this is based on his (peace be upon him) abasing himself before Him. Or (it means) by punishing my offspring, or by placing me among the ranks of the misguided through not granting me success in faith. And it (al-khizy) is from al-khizy in the sense of humiliation (al-hawan), or from al-khizaya in the sense of shame (al-haya').

﴿The day they are raised﴾ — i.e., all of mankind. The pronoun is used before its antecedent because of the widespread fame that the general resurrection enjoys, which renders mention of it unnecessary. Restricting it to the misguided would undermine the awe-inspiring nature of the Day.

Translation of the passage:

﴿On the Day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "the Day when they are resurrected" (yawma yub'athun). It is brought in to emphasize the terror (li-l-tahwil) and to prepare for the exception that follows it (li-ma ya'qubuhu min al-istithna'). It is among the most general of the objects (min a'amm al-mafa'il), meaning:

Wealth does not avail, even if it was spent in the world on the paths of righteousness and good works, and children do not avail, even if they were righteous and deserving of intercession for anyone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 89:

﴿Except for one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾, i.e., free from the sickness of disbelief and hypocrisy, since it is necessary that the benefit of each of them be conditioned on faith. This supports the view that his (peace and blessings be upon him) seeking forgiveness for his father was a request for his guidance to faith, because it is impossible to seek forgiveness for someone who died in disbelief, and he (peace and blessings be upon him) knew that it would not benefit him, since it falls under the category of intercession. It has been said: it is an exception from the subject of "will benefit," with an omitted modifier, i.e., "except the wealth or children of one who comes to God..." (the verse). It has also been said: the omitted modifier is not of the same genus as the excepted term in the strict sense, but rather by a kind of figurative consideration, as in his saying:

....

"A greeting among them is a painful blow,"

i.e., except the state of one who comes to God with a sound heart, where "sound" is an expression for the soundness of the heart, as if it were said: except the soundness of the heart of one who comes to God... (the verse). It has also been said: the omitted modifier is what is indicated by "wealth and children" of richness, and this is the excepted term, as if it were said: "the day when wealth will not benefit, except the richness of one who comes to God..." (the verse), because a person's richness lies in his religion, through the soundness of his heart. It has also been said: the exception is disjunctive, and the meaning is: "But the soundness of his heart will benefit him."

And the Garden will be brought near for those who are mindful (of God) [﴿وَأُزْلِفَتِ الجَنَّةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾], coordinated (ʿatf) with "لا يَنْفَعُ" (will not benefit). The use of the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) in this clause and in the clauses that follow it, which are linked to it in the same conjunctive series, serves to indicate the certainty of the occurrence and its being firmly established, just as the use of the present tense in the clause coordinated-upon (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayh) serves to indicate the continuation and perpetuity of the absence of benefit, as the context of awe-inspiring terror and dreadful depiction requires. That is: the Garden has been brought near to those who are mindful (of God), who have guarded themselves against disbelief and sins, in such a way that they see it from the place of standing (al-mawqif) and become aware of what it contains of the various kinds of excellences, so they rejoice that they are the ones who will be gathered toward it.

And Hell is brought forth for the deviators (al-ghawin), those who went astray from the path of truth, which is faith and God-consciousness (taqwa). That is, it is made manifest to them, such that they see it along with the various terrifying conditions within it, and they become certain that they will be cast into it, and they will find no escape from it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary)) on surah 26, verses 92–93:**

﴿It will be said to them: "Where is that which you used to worship"﴾ in the world ﴿"besides Allah?"﴾ i.e., where are your gods that you used to claim in the world would be your intercessors in this station?

﴿"Can they help you"﴾ by repelling the punishment from you ﴿"or can they help themselves"﴾ by repelling it from themselves?
