**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary)) on surah 26, verses 92–93:**

﴿It will be said to them: "Where is that which you used to worship"﴾ in the world ﴿"besides Allah?"﴾ i.e., where are your gods that you used to claim in the world would be your intercessors in this station?

﴿"Can they help you"﴾ by repelling the punishment from you ﴿"or can they help themselves"﴾ by repelling it from themselves?

This is a question of rebuke and reproach, for which no answer is expected. Therefore it is said: ﴿So they will be thrown headlong into it﴾, meaning: they will be cast into the Hellfire on their faces, again and again, until they settle at its bottom.

﴿They﴾, that is, their deities, ﴿and the misguided ones﴾ who used to worship them. The delaying of mention of them (the misguided ones) after mention of their deities (p-252)

contains a hint that they will be placed after them in the tumbling (al-kabkabah) so that they may witness the wretched state of those deities, and thus their grief will be added to their grief.

{And the hosts of Iblis} — that is, his devils, who used to incite them, whisper to them, and make attractive to them what they were upon of worshipping idols and all the varieties of disbelief and sins, so that they would be gathered together in the punishment just as they had been gathered together in what necessitates it. And it has been said: his followers from the disobedient of the two species (jinn and humankind). The first is the more apparent view.

"Ajma'in" (all of them) is an emphatic (ta'kid) for the pronoun and what is conjoined to it.

This is the continuation of the commentary on the verse. "They say" (qalu) and what follows is a resumptive (isti'naf) clause, which came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of their situation. It is as if it were said: "What did they say when what was done to them was done?" So it was said: the worshippers said, ﴿and they, therein, will dispute﴾, meaning: they said, acknowledging their error in their immersion in misguidance, full of regret, reproaching themselves, while they are in Hellfire on the verge of disputing with those among the aforementioned who are with them, addressing their objects of worship. This is on the basis that God Most High makes the idols capable of disputing, by granting them the power of understanding and speech.

Quran 26:97: ﴿By Allah, we were certainly in clear error.﴾

"In" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna", whose noun, which is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), has been omitted, and the lam is a distinguishing particle (lām al-fāriqah) between it and the negative "in" (al-nāfiyah). The meaning is: indeed the matter is that we were in manifest error. The describing of the error as manifest is for the sake of emphasis (li'l-ish'ā'), in displaying their regret and grief and in explaining the greatness of their mistake in their opinion, despite the clarity of the truth, as is indicated by their opening of the oath with the letter "tā'" (tā'), which conveys amazement (ta'ajjub).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 98:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When We made you equal to the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) modifying "they were in manifest error." It has also been said that it modifies what the speech indicates, that is: "we were astray." It has also been said that it modifies the error mentioned, although there is a grammatical weakness (du'f sina'i) in this, in that a verbal noun (masdar) that has been described cannot govern after the description. It has also been said that it is a temporal clause modifying "manifest" (mubin). The use of the present tense (sighat al-mudari') is to make the past scene present in the mind (istihdar al-surah al-madiyah), that is: "By God, we were indeed in the utmost gross error at the time we made you equal, O idols, in deserving worship, with the Lord of the worlds, who is the lowest of His creatures, the most guided by them, and the most incapable of them."

The statement of theirs, ﴿And none led us astray except the criminals﴾, is an explanation of the cause of their going astray after their acknowledgment that it proceeded from them. However, it is not in the sense of restricting the leading astray to the criminals to the exclusion of others; rather, it is in the sense of restricting their own going astray to being caused by their leading others astray, without their being independently responsible for its occurrence; or that it is caused by the leading astray of others. It is as if it were said: "That gross straying did not proceed from us except because of their leading us astray."

By "the criminals who led them astray" is meant their leaders and their elders, as in His exalted saying: ﴿Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and our elders, and they led us astray from the way﴾. And from al-Suddi, may Allah have mercy on him: "They are the earlier ones whom they followed." Whatever the case, it contains the greatest share of allusion to those who said, ﴿Nay, we found our fathers doing thus﴾.

And from Ibn Jurayj (p. 253): "They are Iblis and the son of Adam who killed, for he was the first to establish killing and various kinds of sins."
Qur'an 26:100: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾, as the believers have from among the angels and the prophets, may blessings and peace be upon them.

Verse 101: ﴿Nor a close friend.﴾ That is, as we see them having friends; or, "Then we have no intercessors, nor a close friend" from among those whom we used to regard as intercessors and friends. Here the absence of these is a metaphor (kinayah) for their enmity, just as the absence of love in the words of God Most High, ﴿God does not love corruption﴾, is a metaphor for hatred, as indicated by His words, Most High: ﴿Intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing.﴾ Or, "We have fallen into a destruction from which no intercessor and no friend will rescue us," the intended meaning of their absence being the absence of their effect. The intercessor (shafi') is given in the plural (shufa'), by way of the frequency of intercessors in common usage, just as the singular of friend (sadiq) is used either because of its scarcity, or because its application to the plural is correct, like 'aduww (enemy), by likening these two to verbal nouns (masadir) such as hanin (longing) and qabul (acceptance).

The word "law" (لَوْ, the conditional particle) in His saying, ﴿So if only we had a return (karrah)﴾, is used to express wishing (tamanni, the expression of a wish), like "layt" (لَيْتَ, "if only"), because there is a meeting between their two meanings in the sense of supposition and hypothesis. It is as if it were said: "So if only we had a return (karrah)," that is, a return to the world. It was also said that it remains in its original sense of a conditional (shart), and its response (jawab) is omitted, as if it were said: "So if we had a return, we would do such-and-such good deeds." This is contradicted by His saying, ﴿and we would be among the believers﴾, because it is necessary for it to be the response to the wish, indicating that their faith is arranged upon the occurrence of the return absolutely, without exception, as their situation requires. Its conjunction to "karrah" follows the manner of "lalubsu 'abā'atin wa taqarra 'aynī" (the wearing of a cloak and the cooling of my eye). As the original sense of "law" requires, it only indicates the realization of the content of the response on the assumption that their return and their faith both occur together, without any indication that the return necessarily entails faith at all, although that is certainly the intended meaning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 103:

﴿And leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses﴾ for the sake of your enjoyment. The word "min" (from) in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿of your spouses﴾ is for specification (bayan) if by it is meant the class of females, which is the apparent meaning; and it is for partition (tab'id) if by it is meant the permissible part of them, as an allusion that they used to do this with their wives as well.

﴿Nay, you are a people transgressing﴾ exceeding the limit, going beyond bounds in all acts of disobedience, and this is among them. It has also been said: going beyond the limit of desire, in that they exceeded all other people, and even the animals.

They said, "If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be among those expelled."

That is, [desist] from denouncing our command and forbidding [them] from it, or from claiming prophethood, one of whose rulings is confronting us.

"Among those expelled" means among those banished from our town; and it seems they used to expel whomever they expelled from their homes with violence and ill treatment.

Translation:

﴿He said: "Indeed, I am of those who detest your deed"﴾. That is: of those who hate it to the utmost degree, as if he burns (يُقْلِي) the heart and the liver because of its intensity. And this is more emphatic than saying "I am one who detests your deed" (إنِّي لِعَمَلِكم قالٍ), because it indicates that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is among the company of those firmly established in that (hatred) and renowned for their detestation of it.

And perhaps he, upon him be prayer and peace, intended to show his aversion to dwelling among them and his desire to be delivered from the evil of their neighbourhood. For this reason he turned away from debating with them and addressed God Most High, saying: ﴿My Lord, deliver me and my family from what they do﴾, that is, from the ill consequence of their deeds and its harm.

﴿So We saved him and his family, all of them﴾. That is: the people of his household and those who followed him in the religion, by bringing them out from among them (the people) when the punishment was about to descend upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 171:

﴿Except an old woman﴾ is the wife of Lot. She was excepted from his family, so the fact that she was an unbeliever does not harm his standing, because she had a share in the family status by the right of marriage.

﴿Among those who remained behind﴾ means: it was decreed that she would be among those who remained in the punishment, because she was inclined toward the people and pleased with their deed. The stone struck her on the road and destroyed her, as has passed in (Surat al-Hijr) and (Surat Hud). It is also said: she was among those who stayed behind in the town and did not leave with Lot, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 172:

﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ We annihilated them with the most severe and dreadful destruction.

And We rained down upon them a rain (﴿وَأمْطَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ مَطَرًا﴾). That is, a rain unlike the usual kind. It has been said: God rained down stones upon the most wayward of the people, and they destroyed them.

﴿فَساءَ مَطَرُ المُنْذَرِينَ﴾ — "Evil is the rain of those who were warned." The alif-lam in "al-Mundharin" is for the genus (lam al-jins), and by it the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) can serve as the subject (fa'il) of sa'a (the verb of evil). The noun specified by the dispraise (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted, and it is "maṭaruhum" (their rain).

Ask, in the wording of the verse: "Give full measure" (﴿Give full measure﴾), that is, complete it. "And do not be of those who cause loss" (﴿and do not be of those who cause loss﴾), that is, by cheating people of their rights through short-measure (tatfif).

"And do not deprive people of their things" — that is, do not diminish anything of their rights, whatever right it may be. This is a generalization after the specific mention of some matters, because of how thoroughly they were absorbed in them.

﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing corruption﴾ — through killing, raiding, and highway robbery.

["And fear Him who created you and the earlier generations."] That is, [fear] the possessors of the earlier generations, namely those who came before you of the creatures. Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 187:

﴿So cause fragments of the sky to fall upon us﴾, i.e., pieces. It is also read with a sukun on the sin (ḥarf al-sīn), and this is likewise the plural of kisfah. It has been said: al-kisf and al-kisfah are like al-rīʿ and al-rīʿah, meaning a piece. By "the sky" is meant either the clouds or a canopy. Perhaps this is a response to what was implied by the command to be wary (al-taqawwī) of the threat. (p-263)

﴿If you are among the truthful﴾ in your claim. Their request was only due to their insistence upon denial and rejection, and had it not been so, they would not have entertained it in their minds, let alone requested it.

Shu'ayb... no, the passage is about Shu'ayb's people's reply? Here the passage is Shu'ayb's response in verse 188 (the people asked him to make the punishment fall, and he said): 

"He said: My Lord knows best what you do" — referring to disbelief and sins, and what punishment you deserve because of it; so He will send it down upon you at its appointed time, without fail.

**﴿So they denied him⦆** meaning: they persisted in denying him and insisted upon it.

**﴿So the punishment of the Day of the Shade seized them﴾** in accordance with what they had demanded. As for whether they meant by "the sky" the clouds, this is evident; and as for whether they meant the canopy, it is because the punishment descended from it. The attribution of the punishment to "the Day of the Shade" rather than to the shade itself indicates that on that day they suffered another punishment besides the punishment of the shade: namely, God subjected them to the heat for seven days and nights, and it seized their breaths, so that neither shade, nor water, nor a cool place benefited them. They were compelled to go out into the open country, and a cloud overshadowed them; they found in it coolness and a breeze, so they gathered beneath it, and it rained fire upon them, and they were all burned. It is narrated that Shu'ayb, upon him be peace, was sent to two communities: the People of Madyan and the People of al-Aykah. Madyan was destroyed by the Cry and the Earthquake, and the People of al-Aykah by the punishment of the Day of the Shade.

**﴿Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous Day﴾** meaning: in its severity and terror, and the dreadfulness of what befell them therein of calamity and complete catastrophe.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 26, verses 190–191:**

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.﴾ This is the end of the seven stories that were revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), in order to turn him (ﷺ) away from being eager for the Islam of his people, to cut off his hope in them, and to remove his grief over their missing out on it. This fulfills what was mentioned at the opening of the noble surah, in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿No new reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿They have indeed denied the truth...﴾ up to the verse. Each of these stories was mentioned as an independent account, newly revealed, which had come to them from Him, Exalted is He, by the necessity of His vast mercy. "And most of them were not believers" after they heard them in detail, story after story, not in the sense that they reflected upon them and took lessons from what each one contains of incentives to faith and deterrents from disbelief and transgression, nor in the sense that they contemplated the matter of the noble verses that narrate those stories as they are, while knowing that he (ﷺ) had never heard any of them from anyone at all. Instead, they continued in the disbelief and misguidance they were in, as if they had heard nothing that would restrain them from it, decisively, as has been established at the conclusion of the story of Moses, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 192:

﴿And indeed it﴾ — i.e., what has been mentioned of the noble verses, which narrate the stories related, or the Qur'an of which they are a part — ﴿is the revelation of the Lord of the worlds﴾ — i.e., sent down from His direction, may He be exalted. It is called "tanzil" (revelation) by way of emphasis (mubalaghah). And describing Him, may He be exalted, with the lordship (rububiyyah) of the worlds is to indicate (li-l-idhan) that its being sent down is among the rulings of His exalted nurturing (tarbiyah) and His compassion (ra'fah) toward all, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ (p-264).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 193:

﴿Nazala bihi﴾ means: He sent it down. ﴿al-Ruhu al-Amin﴾ means: Jibril (peace be upon him), for he is the trustworthy one of His revelation (amin wahyihi) and the one who conveys it to His prophets, may prayers and peace be upon them.

It is also read with the zay shaddah (tashdid) and with the ruh and amin in the accusative (nasb), meaning: Allah, may He be exalted, made the Trustworthy Spirit descend with it (ja'ala Allahu ta'ala al-Ruha al-Amina nazilan bihi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 194:

﴿عَلى قَلْبِكَ﴾ That is: your spirit (ruh). Even if it is meant as the physical organ, its specification is because the spiritual meanings descend first upon the spirit, then pass from it to the heart because of the connection between them, then ascend to the brain, where the tablet of the imaginative faculty (lawh al-mutakhayyilah) is imprinted by them.

﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ المُنْذِرِينَ﴾ This is connected to "nazala bihi" (it descended with it). That is: He sent it down so that you may warn them with what it contains of terrible punishments. The choice of the wording used in the noble arrangement is to indicate that you (ﷺ) are included in the line of those well-known warners concerning the truth of the message and the certainty of the occurrence of the warning punishment.

Qur'an 26:195: "in clear Arabic speech" (bi-lisanin 'arabiyyin mubin). Its meaning is plain and its significance evident, so that no excuse remains for them. It is also connected to "revealed it" (nazala bihi), and its being placed later serves to give attention to the matter of warning, and to indicate that the basis for his being among the warners mentioned, peace be upon them, is merely the fact that it was sent down to him (ﷺ), not that it was sent down in the Arabic tongue.

Connecting it to "the warners," as the majority (al-Jumhur) permitted, would lead to the conclusion that the ultimate purpose of the revelation was his (ﷺ) being among the warners in the Arabic language only, alongside Hud, Salih and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them. Its corruption is not hidden. How could it be otherwise, when the greatest of all warnings is what Noah and Moses, peace be upon them both, delivered, and the most effective of admonitions upon the hearts of the polytheists is what Abraham, peace be upon him, warned of, because they claimed affiliation with him and asserted that they were upon his creed, peace and blessings be upon him?

And indeed it is in the Scriptures of the earlier peoples (﴿وَإنَّهُ لَفي زُبُرِ الأوَّلِينَ﴾). That is: indeed its mention, or its meaning, is in the earlier books. For its rulings, which do not admit abrogation (naskh, the replacing of one ruling by another) or alteration (tabdil) according to the changing of the ages, namely the affirmation of the Oneness of God (tawhid) and all that pertains to the Essence and the Attributes, are written down in them. Likewise [written in them] is what is within its folds of admonitions and narratives. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but this is not clear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 197:

﴿Has it not been a sign for them﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial and negation, and the waw is for conjunction, coordinating with an implied element required by the context. It is as if it were said: "Did they neglect this, and was there not for them a sign indicating that it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, and that it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples?" As for "for them" (lahum), it is related to the existence (al-kawn, the verb "to be" as a complete predicate) and placed before its subject and predicate for emphasis on it. Or it is related to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "a sign" (ayatan), and it was placed before it because "a sign" is indefinite (nakira).

"A sign" (ayatun) is the predicate of the existence (al-kawn), placed before its subject, which is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it﴾, because of the attention and arousing of anticipation toward what is delayed, as has been mentioned many times. That is: that they should know it by its described attributes mentioned in their books, and that they should recognize the one upon whom it was sent down.

It has been read as "takun" with the feminine marker, and "ayatun" is then taken as the subject and "an ya'lamahu" as the predicate. In this there is weakness, since an indefinite noun occurs as the subject and a definite one as the predicate. It has been said that in "takun" the pronoun is that of the matter (damir al-qissa, the anaphoric pronoun of the story), and "ayatan an ya'lamahu" is a clause occupying the place of the predicate. It is also permissible that "lahum ayatun" be the clause of the matter (jumlat al-sha'n), and that "an ya'lamahu" be a substitute (badal) for "ayatun". It is also permissible, with "ayatan" in the accusative, to have the feminine "takun" as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then their trial was not but that they said﴾. It has also been read as "ta'lamahu" with the letter ta'.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 198:

﴿And if We had sent it down﴾ as it is, with its striking and inimitable composition, ﴿upon one of the non-Arabs﴾ (al-a'jamin), those who are unable to speak Arabic. It is the plural of a'jami (non-Arab), formed with a lightened (takhfif) pattern, and for this reason it takes the sound plural form. It has also been read as "al-a'jamiyyin." The word "some" (ba'd) in the phrase indicates that this (person) would be one of the ordinary members of that group, whoever he might be.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 199:

﴿So he recited it to them﴾ with a correct recitation that breaks customary norms, ﴿yet they would not have believed in it﴾, with the miraculousness of the recitation joined to the miraculousness of what is recited, due to the extreme of their obstinacy and the severity of their disposition in stubborn denial. It has been said: the meaning is: Had We sent it down upon one of the non-Arabs (a'jamiyyin), in the language of the non-Arabs, so that he recited it to them, they would not have believed in it, due to their not understanding it and their disdain for following the non-Arabs. But this is not so, for it is far from the appropriate context of explaining their persistence in stubborn denial and obstinacy.

Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals (al-mujrimin), meaning: in the same manner as that wonderful insertion just mentioned, We have caused the Qur'an to enter into the hearts of the criminals. So they understood its meanings and recognized its eloquence, and that it is beyond the capacities of human beings in terms of its miraculous composition (nazm) and in terms of its reports of the unseen (al-ghayb). To this was joined the agreement of the scholars of the earlier revealed Scriptures that it contains glad tidings of its descent and of the sending of the one to whom it was revealed, with his attributes.

Then His saying, ﴿They will not believe in it﴾, is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah), brought to explain that they are not affected by the likes of those matters that call to belief in it, but rather they persist in what they are upon. ﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾, which compels them to belief in it at a time when belief will not benefit them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 202:

﴿So it will come upon them suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, in this world and in the Hereafter, ﴿while they perceive not﴾ its coming.

﴿فَيَقُولُوا هَلْ نَحْنُ مُنْظَرُونَ﴾ [So they will say: "Will we be given respite?"] expressing remorse over what was lost of faith and a wish for a reprieve to make up for what they neglected. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿كَذَلِكَ سَلَكْناهُ﴾ [Thus We caused it to enter] is: in the likeness of that state and that attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it, We placed it in their hearts. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ [they do not believe in it] is in the position of clarification and summation of it, or in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: We caused it to enter them while they did not believe in it. The first is the more fitting for the context of declaring the extreme of their obstinacy and arrogance, together with the mutual support of the proofs of faith, the convergence of the principles of guidance and direction, and the complete cutting off of their excuses. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿سَلَكْناهُ﴾ refers to disbelief, which is indicated by what precedes it, namely His statement, exalted is He, "they were not believers in it." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid (may Allah have mercy on them both), that it means: We caused polytheism and denial to enter the hearts of the guilty. (p-266)

Is it then for Our punishment that they seek to hasten? By their saying, "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment," and their saying, "Then bring us what you promise us..." and the like. Their state at the descent of the punishment is as He described, in their seeking to be warned. The **fa'** (الفاء, the conjunctive particle) here coordinates with an implied clause demanded by the context. That is: "Will their state be as mentioned, of seeking respite at the descent of the painful punishment, so that they hasten for Our punishment, when the contradiction between the two is clear to everyone? Or are they heedless of that, though it is certain and established, so that they hasten, etc.?" The **prepositional phrase** (الجار والمجرور, al-jar wa'l-majrur) was placed first to indicate that the focus of the denunciation and rebuke is that what they hasten for is His punishment, together with what it entails of observing the **fawasil** (فواصل, the rhyming verse-endings).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 205:

﴿Have you considered?﴾ Since sight is among the strongest and most widely known means of knowing something, the usage of *a-ra-ayta* (have you considered) came to mean: inform me. The address is to everyone who is fit to receive it, whoever he may be. The *fa'* (then) indicates the sequence of the questioning after their words: "Are we to be reprieved?" What lies between them is an *i'tiraD* (parenthetical insertion) for rebuke and reproach, and it precedes the *hamza* (interrogative particle) in meaning. Its placement after the *hamza* in form is because the *hamza* requires initial position in the sentence, as is the view of the *jumhur* (majority of scholars). That is: then inform me, ﴿if We let them enjoy for years﴾, extended by the length of their lifespans and the pleasantness of their livelihood.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 206:

﴿Then there came to them that which they had been promised﴾ of the punishment.

﴿What did it avail them?﴾ "What" (ayy shay') or "what kind of availing" (ayy igh'na') did it avail them, ﴿what they were given enjoyment of﴾. That is, their being given that lasting enjoyment, on the basis that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (ma masdariyyah); or "what they were given enjoyment with of the provisions of the worldly life," on the basis that it is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted. In either case the interrogation is for denial and negation. It has also been said that "ma" is a negative particle, meaning: their prolonged enjoyment did not avail them in repelling or lightening the punishment. The first view is the preferable one, because it better fits the form of the interrogation and is more indicative of the negation of benefit in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, as if every addressee were charged with informing that their enjoyment benefited them in what way, and what availed them, yet none could say anything of that at all. It is also read as "yumatti'una" (yumatti'ūn), from the causative form (al-imta').

Translation:

"And We did not destroy any town" [of the towns that were destroyed] "except that it had warners" [who had already warned its people, so as to establish the proof against them].

﴿Dhikra﴾ means a reminder (tadhkira). Its grammatical position is the accusative (naṣb), either as a reason (ʿilla, "cause" or "purpose") or as an infinitive (maṣdar), because it carries the sense of warning (al-inḏār). It is as if it were said: "They warn as a reminder." Or it is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar muʾakkid) for a verb that is a description of "munḏirūn," meaning: "except that there were warners for them who remind them, a reminder." Or it is in the nominative (rafʿ), either because it is a description of "munḏirūn" with an implied "ḏawū" (possessors of), or by treating them as a reminder because of their thoroughness in reminding, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, in which case the sentence is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya). The pronoun in "lahā" refers to "al-qurā" (the towns), which is understood from its singular form falling within the scope of negation, on the basis that the meaning "for all there are warners" is more general than whether each town has one warner or more.

﴿And We were not wrongdoers﴾, so that We would destroy those who are not wrongdoers. It has been said that the warning and the expression of it by negating wrongdoing, although their destruction before the warning is not wrongdoing at all according to what is established in the principle of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school of theology), is to show the perfection of His transcendence above that by portraying it in the form of what is impossible for Him to do, namely wrongdoing. This has passed in Surat Al ʿImran at His saying: ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾.

﴿And the devils have not brought it down.﴾ This is a refutation of the claim made by the disbelievers concerning the Noble Qur'an, that it is of the same kind as what Satan casts to the soothsayers (kahanah), after the truth has been established by the statement that the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down.
And it is not befitting for them ﴿وَما يَنْبَغِي لَهُمْ﴾: that is, it is neither proper nor fitting for them to do that, ﴿وَما يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾ and they are not at all able to do it.

Verse 212: ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾ — from the words of the angels — ﴿they are indeed removed﴾, because there is no shared ground between them and the angels in the purity of essences and in the readiness to receive the outpouring of the lights of Truth and to be imprinted with the forms of divine sciences and luminous knowledge. How could it be otherwise, when their souls are wicked, dark, evil by nature, and disposed only to receive that which contains no good whatsoever, of all kinds of evil? So how could they ever hover around the Noble Qur'an, which contains refined, unseen truths that can be received only from the angels, upon them be prayer and peace?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 213:

﴿So do not invoke another god alongside Allah, lest you be among those who are punished.﴾ This was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), although it is evident that what is forbidden could not possibly proceed from him (ﷺ). It serves to stir him and urge him to increase in sincerity (ikhlas), and it serves as a kindness to the rest of the responsible persons (mukallafin) by making clear that association (shirk) is so ugly and evil that one who could never commit it is forbidden from it, so how much more so anyone else.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 214:

﴿And warn﴾ of the punishment that follows from polytheism (shirk) and sins, ﴿your closest kinsmen﴾, beginning with the nearest of them, then the next nearest, for concern for their affair is most important. It is narrated that when it was revealed, he (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and called out to them clan by clan (fakhdan fakhdan) until they gathered around him. He said: "If I told you that at the foot of this mountain there were horsemen, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment."

And it is narrated that he said: "O sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of Hashim, O sons of 'Abd Manaf, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything. Then he said: "O 'A'isha, daughter of Abu Bakr, O Hafsa, daughter of 'Umar, O Fatima, daughter of Muhammad, O Safiyya, aunt of Muhammad: buy yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot avail you anything."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 215:

﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers.﴾ (p-268) That is: soften your side toward them. It is a metaphor taken from the state of a bird, for when it wishes to descend it lowers its wing. The "min" (مَن) in "لِمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ" is for specification (lil-tabyin), because "those who follow you" (مَن اتَّبَعَ) is more general than "those who followed you for the sake of religion or otherwise." Or it is for partition (lil-tab'id), on the basis that the intended meaning of "the believers" (المُؤْمِنِينَ) is those who are on the verge of faith, or those who merely affirm it verbally.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 216:

﴿Then if they disobey you﴾ and do not follow you, ﴿say: "Indeed, I am free of what you do"﴾. That is: of what you do, or of your deeds.

﴿And put your trust in the Mighty, the Merciful﴾, who is able to subdue His enemies and grant victory to His allies. He will suffice you against the evil of those among them, and of others, who disobey you. It was also read as "فَتَوَكَّلَ" (fa-tawakkal), on the basis that it is a *badal* (substitution, or apposition) for the *jawab al-shart* (the response clause of the conditional).
﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ — that is, to the tahajjud (voluntary night prayer).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 219:

﴿And your turning about among those who prostrate﴾: and your moving back and forth in examining the states of those who pray at night (tahajjud), as it is narrated that when the obligation of the night prayer (qiyam al-layl) was abrogated (naskh), he (ﷺ) (ﷺ) went around the houses of his Companions that night to see what they were doing, out of eagerness for the abundance of their worship. He found them like the houses of hornets, because of the humming (dandaana) he heard from them in the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and in recitation.

Or it means your movement among those praying, with standing, bowing, prostration and sitting, when you lead them in prayer.

Allah the Exalted described Himself as knowing his state (ﷺ) by which he deserves His guardianship (wilaya), after He had expressed Him by what points to the subduing of his enemies and the victory of his friends, through the two attributes al-'Aziz (the Almighty) and al-Rahim (the Most Merciful), in order to confirm reliance (tawakkul) and to settle his heart upon it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 220:

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what they utter, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what they intend and conceal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 221:

﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ That is: "tatanazzalu" (they descend), with one of the two tā' elided. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the impossibility of the devils descending upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after the explanation of the impossibility of their descending with the Qur'an.

As for the entry of the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) upon "man" (interrogative "who"): this is because it is not originally placed for interrogation; rather the original form is "amman," and the interrogative particle was elided, and usage continued with its elision, just as it was elided from "hal," whose original form is "ahl."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 222:

And His saying, ﴿Upon every lying, sinful one do they descend﴾, is a restriction (qasr) of their descent to every one who is characterized by much lying (ifk) and great sin (ithm), from among the soothsayers (kahana) and the false prophetesses (mutanabbi'a), and a specification of it to them, such that it does not pass beyond them to others. And since the court of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is exalted above any trace of those attributes coming near it, the impossibility of their descent upon him (ﷺ) has become clear.

﴿They cast﴾, i.e., the liars (al-Affakun), ﴿the hearing﴾ (p-269) to the devils, so they receive from them illusions and indications because of their deficiency of knowledge, and they add to these, in accordance with their false imaginings, fables most of which do not match reality. This is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, i.e., in what they relate of statements. It has been transmitted in a hadith: "A word is snatched by the jinn, who whispers it into the ear of his protégé, and he adds more than a hundred lies to it." Or [the meaning is]: they cast the hearing, i.e., what is heard from the devils, to people, and most of them are liars, fabricating against the devils what they have not revealed to them. The more apparent view is that the majority [in "most of them"] refers to their statements, meaning that these people rarely speak truthfully in what they relate about the jinn, but in most of it they are liars. Its implication is that most of their statements are false, not that their essences are liars, such that attributing lying to most of them would entail that a few of them are truthful absolutely. The meaning of the affak (liar) is not one who speaks only falsehood, such that truthfulness is impossible for him, but rather one who abounds in falsehood, so it is not inconsistent with this that he tells the truth rarely, at some times.

It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the devils, meaning: they cast the hearing, i.e., what is heard from the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) before they are pelted with meteors, from some of the unseen matters, to their protégés, and most of them are liars in what they reveal to them, since they do not hear them in the manner in which the angels spoke, owing to their wickedness, or to the deficiency of their understanding, or their retention, or their conveying [of the message]. There is no way to interpret the casting of the hearing as their eavesdropping and listening to the Exalted Assembly before the pelting, as the majority (al-Jumhur) permitted, since [the verb] "they cast" (yulqun), as they have stated, is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "descended" (tanazzalu), indicating that the descent is concurrent with the casting, or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the purpose of the descent, built upon the question about it. There is no doubt that casting the hearing to the Exalted Assembly is far from the possibility of being concurrent with the descent or being its purpose, since it definitely precedes it. What is possible for both is the casting in the first sense. So the meaning, on the assumption that it is a circumstantial clause, is: the descent of the devils upon the liars, casting to them what they heard from the Exalted Assembly. On the assumption that it is an answer to the question of one who says, "Why do they descend upon them, and what do they do with them?", [the answer is]: they cast to them what they heard. To take it as a resumptive report, as some have done, is not correct, because mentioning their states prior to the descent mentioned before it is not befitting the eloquence of the revelation (al-tanzil).

As for the assumption that the pronoun in "they cast" refers to the liars, then it is a description of every liar, because it has the sense of the plural, whether the casting of the hearing means listening to the devils or casting what is heard to people. It is permissible that it be a resumptive report about their condition on both assumptions, since each of their receiving from the devils and their casting to people occurs after the revelation. It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause built upon the question on the first assumption only, as if it were said: "What do they do when the devils descend upon them?" It is answered: "They cast their hearing to them so that they may memorize what is revealed to them." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, on the first assumption, is only a resumptive clause; on the second, it may be circumstantial from the pronoun in "they cast", i.e., what they heard from the devils to people, while the state is that in most of their statements they are liars. So reflect.

This is a commentary passage (Abu al-Su'ud's Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 26, verse 224.

﴿And the poets—those who go astray follow them.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that picks up the argument), brought to refute what they said about the Noble Qur'an, namely that it is of the category of poetry, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is one of the poets. It does so by describing the state of the poets, which is contrary to his state (ﷺ), after having refuted their claim that it is of the category of the falsehoods that the devils cast upon the soothsayers (kahanah), through what has passed of the explanation of their states, which are opposed to his states (ﷺ).

The meaning is: the poets are followed by them, that is, they are accompanied and their path is taken, and among their number are "those who go astray" (al-ghawun), those who deviate from the way (al-sunan), who are bewildered in what they do and what they leave undone, who do not persist on one uniform course in their actions, sayings and states. Not so the others, the people of right guidance (al-rushd), who are rightly guided to the path of truth and firm upon it.

(p-270)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 225:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ It is a testimony to the fact that the poets are only followed by the deviators, and a confirmation of it. The address is to everyone from whom sight can be expected, with the aim of showing that their state is so clear and manifest that the seeing is not restricted to one viewer rather than another. That is: Have you not seen that the poets, in every valley of the valleys of idle talk and gossip (qil wa-qal), and in every ravine of the ravines of illusion and imagination, and in every path of the paths of error and misguidance, wander aimlessly, not guided to any specific one of the ways, but rather bewildered in the wastelands of deviation and foolishness, and lost in the perplexity of licentiousness and shamelessness. Their religion is the tearing apart of protected honors, the slandering of pure and noble lineages, erotic poetry about the forbidden (nasib bi-l-haram), amorous verse (ghazal), and profligacy (ibtiyar), and vacillation between the two extremes of excess and deficiency in praise and satire.

﴿And as for them, they say what they do not do.﴾ [They do so] in matters of action, being indifferent to the reproach that follows from it. How, then, could it be imagined that he (ﷺ) would follow them on that path, join them, and be counted in their ranks? His sacred precinct is far removed from even a trace of attachment to any of the matters mentioned. He is characterized by noble qualities and adorned with beautiful moral excellences. He has attained all sacred perfections and won the full range of human virtues. He is steadfast upon the straight path and persevering upon the upright way, speaking every right matter and calling to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy. He is supported by overpowering miracles and manifest signs, filled with the arts of dazzling wisdom and kinds of radiant knowledge, and standing alone in a fine composition that defeated every skilled logician and put to shame every sorcerous eloquent poet.

This has been said regarding his (ﷺ) exemption from being among the poets: that the followers of poets are the deviators, and the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ) are not like that. There is no doubt that justifying his (ﷺ) not being among them by the fact that his followers are not deviators is something not befitting his exalted station.

It was said: al-Ghawun (the deviators) are the transmitters (al-ruwat). It was said: they are the devils. It was said: they are the poets of Quraysh: Abdullah ibn al-Za'bara, Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb al-Makhzumi, Musafi' ibn Abd Manaf, and Abu 'Izza al-Jumahi; and from Thaqif, Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. They said: "We say the like of what Muhammad (ﷺ) says."

It was read: "wa-al-shu'ara'" (والشُّعَراءُ) in the accusative, by supposing an implied verb that the apparent one explains. It was read: "yattabi'uhum" (يَتْبَعُهُمْ) with lightening (takhfif, the removal of the doubled letter), and "yatba'hum" (يَتْبَعْهُمْ) with the ʿayn vowelless, likening some forms to others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 26, verse 227:

﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged.﴾ This is an exception for the believing, righteous poets, who remember Allah, Mighty and Majestic, often, and whose poetry is mostly about divine unity (tawhid), praise of Allah the Exalted, urging obedience to Him, wisdom and admonition, asceticism in this world, encouraging people to turn away from relying on it, and warning against being deceived by its adornments and seduced by its fleeting pleasures. And if some of them at times produced satire, it was in the manner of retaliation against those who had satirized them. It has been said: the ones meant by the exception are ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha, Hassan ibn Thabit, Ka'b ibn Malik, and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr ibn Abi (p-271) Sulma, and those who used to defend the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and confront the satirists of Quraysh. It is reported on the authority of Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he (ﷺ) used to say to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you."

﴿And those who have done wrong will come to know what sort of return they will be returned to.﴾ This is a severe threat and a firm warning, due to the awe-inspiring nature of its object in "will come to know" (sa-ya'lamu), and in ﴿those who have done wrong﴾ there is generality and inclusiveness, and in ﴿what sort of return they will be returned to﴾ there is vagueness and awe-inspiring force. Abu Bakr said this to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was appointed (as caliph). It was also read as "ayya munfalatin yanfalituna" (what sort of escape they will escape), from the root infilat, meaning deliverance. The meaning is: the wrongdoers hope to escape the punishment of Allah the Exalted, but they will come to know that there is no way for them to escape.

From the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surat al-Shu'ara' will have ten good deeds recorded for him for each of those who believed in Noah and those who disbelieved in him, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb and Ibrahim, and for each of those who disbelieved in Jesus and believed in Muhammad ﷺ."
